requests.user: {"source":"On the first Saturday of May, twelve neighbors met beside the disused pump house to clean the narrow path to the creek. The path had been passable in winter, but spring grass hid broken glass near the bend. I had brought two rakes and a box of gloves. Lena brought a wheelbarrow with one stiff wheel, which announced every trip back to the gate. We worked for an hour before anyone reached the water. A few people expected the council to collect the filled bags that afternoon. Lena said the council had agreed only to collect them on Monday, provided we stacked them inside the gate. That small detail changed our plan: we stopped filling bags at the creek and carried each one out before starting another. By noon, we had cleared about thirty meters of path. That is my estimate, not a measured distance. We left the last stretch untouched because a nest was visible in the reeds and nobody knew whether birds were using it. After lunch, Arun tied a strip of cloth to a post so walkers would notice the uncleared section. He did not call it a barrier. He was right; a barrier would have made the route look finished on either side. On Monday the bags were gone when I passed the gate. I did not see the collection truck, so I cannot say who removed them. The path is easier to walk now, though the bend still needs attention. Next time I would bring fewer rakes and more gloves. The wheelbarrow can stay, provided someone oils that wheel first.","objective":"Edit this neighborhood field note for a community newsletter; keep its modest, observant first-person voice.","style":{"label":"Natural","description":"Plain, human rhythm. requests.user: {"source":"The museum tested a new wayfinding sheet during four afternoon sessions in June. Visitors received a single folded page at the entrance, with a simple map on one side and room names on the other. The old sheet had listed exhibits alphabetically. Staff suspected that visitors were using it as a checklist rather than a route, but they had no direct evidence of that behavior. For the trial, volunteers offered the new sheet to every third arriving group when the entrance was not crowded. Thirty-six groups accepted it; nine declined. The volunteers did not track groups that arrived during busy periods, so the figures do not describe all visitors. At the exit, twenty accepted groups answered one question about finding the textile gallery. Fifteen said it had been easy, three said it had been difficult, and two were unsure. There was no comparison question for visitors using the old sheet. One volunteer also noticed that several families paused at the stairwell and checked the map twice. Her observation is useful for locating a possible trouble spot, though it does not establish how often the problem occurred. The design team proposes moving the textile gallery arrow closer to the stairwell symbol and testing that change in July. They also want to ask the same exit question of groups using each sheet. If staffing allows, a volunteer will record how many groups skip the sheet entirely. The museum can print another small batch for the July test without changing its permanent signs. A larger print run should wait until staff can compare the two sheets under similar conditions.
